claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature, single-phase BCC alloy.
The transition from high-temperature BCC to a multiphase assemblage is governed by a critical composition-dependent free-energy threshold.
Cooling increases the free-energy driving force for transformation.
Once the free-energy driving force crosses the critical threshold, it overcomes kinetic barriers to nucleation.
Crossing the proposed threshold produces a rapid and reproducible phase transformation.
Cooling shifts the alloy's free-energy landscape.
A sufficiently negative composition-dependent ΔG causes rapid nucleation followed by growth of secondary phases.
The transformation will have a sharp onset at a specific temperature or equivalent ΔG value.
The sharp transformation onset will appear as the sudden emergence and subsequent increase of secondary-phase diffraction peaks.
Under slow-cooling conditions that do not reach the proposed threshold, the high-temperature BCC phase remains stable.
Diffusion kinetics that are too slow can hide the proposed ΔG-threshold effect.
Cooling that is too fast can bypass controlled nucleation and prevent the predicted threshold behavior from being observed.
Minor differences in microstructure or processing history may alter the critical free-energy threshold.
A gradual transformation over a broad temperature range without a reproducible onset would falsify the threshold hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis defines the threshold through composition- and temperature-dependent ΔG, but the baseline implies that slow cooling itself prevents the threshold from being reached. At a matched composition and temperature, cooling rate can alter kinetics but does not by itself determine the thermodynamic ΔG, so the proposed baseline is not internally consistent unless it uses a different terminal temperature.
